name: Raw egg consumption

lead: Raw egg consumption means drinking or eating uncooked eggs, usually blended into shakes, as a cheap protein and choline source for building muscle. It follows the old strongman and Rocky Balboa image and appears on looksmax.org forums.

The chain is protein and choline intake supporting training and muscle gain. Wikipedia reports egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable raw versus roughly 91 percent cooked, so less of the protein is absorbed raw. Forum posts range from people drinking a dozen or more at a time to threads calling raw eggs a meme.

paras: Eggs are blended with milk, banana or protein powder into a shake, usually around training. Some users choose pasteurised eggs. Any muscle effect would arrive through overall protein intake and training over months.

Salmonella can contaminate eggs inside the egg or on a cracked shell, and heat destroys it; case-control research found raw eggs a leading risk factor for Salmonella Enteritidis infection. Health authorities advise vulnerable groups against raw eggs. Raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin, and raw egg allergy reactions have been reported even in people who tolerate cooked egg. Pasteurised eggs are sold as a lower-risk option.

angle.text: Raw eggs go into shakes as inexpensive protein and choline to support training and muscle gain. Research reports lower protein absorption from raw eggs than cooked, and no studies look at appearance.

lead: Raw egg consumption means eating or drinking uncooked eggs, usually cracked into a blender or shaker with milk or protein powder. People do it to add protein, fat and choline to a physique-building diet with no cooking time, an idea tied to strength-sports lore and to the image of Rocky Balboa gulping raw eggs in the 1976 film. Looksmax.org users describe the habit as a cheap, fast way to fuel muscle gain, which they connect to a fuller, leaner and more athletic look.[1][2][3][4]

Two measurable differences between raw and cooked egg are well documented. In a 1998 stable-isotope study of five ileostomy patients, true ileal digestibility of egg protein was about 91 percent when cooked and about 51 percent when raw.[5] And raw egg white contains avidin, a protein that binds the vitamin biotin so tightly that very large raw-white intakes caused hair loss, skin rash and nerve problems in early twentieth-century animal experiments; cooking largely disables avidin.[6][7] Biotin is the vitamin popularly linked to hair, skin and nails, which is why this point recurs in appearance discussions.

Food-safety agencies add a third concern, Salmonella, which can contaminate eggs and is destroyed by heat. The FDA advises using pasteurised eggs or pasteurised egg products in recipes that call for raw egg, and lists children, older adults, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems as being at greater risk of severe illness.[8][9]

A 2022 randomised trial from Maastricht University, titled with a nod to the film, compared five raw eggs, five boiled eggs and a control breakfast after resistance exercise in 45 young men. Raw eggs slowed the rise of amino acids in the blood, yet muscle protein synthesis rose by a similar amount in both egg groups.[10] Forum users cite both sides of this literature, and some pair raw eggs with pasteurisation or with other raw-food habits associated with the ancestral-diet scene.[3][11]

paras: Eggs can be eaten raw, for example blended into a shake, whisked into dressings and desserts, or swallowed whole. Health experts advise against eating them raw, especially for older adults, sick people and pregnant women, who are more vulnerable to salmonellosis.[8] A 2015 review notes that growing consumer interest in raw and unprocessed foods may be raising the risk of salmonellosis.[12]

A medium or large hen's egg weighs roughly 50 g and supplies about 6 g of protein, about 5 g of fat and about 70 kcal, with notable amounts of choline, vitamin B12, riboflavin and pantothenic acid.[8] Eggs score the maximum on the protein digestibility-corrected amino acid score, which is one reason they are a staple of muscle-building diets.[8] Raw-egg drinkers use that profile and skip the cooking step, which they describe as saving time and washing up.[2]

Humans have eaten eggs for a very long time; chickens were likely domesticated for their eggs before 7500 BCE and reached Egypt and Sumer by about 1500 BCE.[8] Raw egg drinks have long been part of folk tonics and old-school strength-training lore, in which strongmen and boxers are said to have swallowed raw eggs before training.

Rocky premiered in New York on 20 November 1976, and its improvised training scenes, including punching sides of beef and running the Philadelphia museum steps, became a template for aspirational training culture.[4] The raw-egg gulp from that film is the usual reference point when people discuss the habit online. The 2022 Maastricht trial borrowed the film's name for its title, asking whether the character 'got it right or wrong'.[10]

The 2020s gave raw eggs a second life in social media diet scenes built around raw milk, organ meats and 'ancestral' eating. Fitness influencer Brian Johnson, known as Liver King, built a large following promoting raw organ meat as part of an ancestral lifestyle, and Wikipedia reports that he later admitted spending large sums on steroids despite earlier denials.[11] Forum users on looksmax.org mention raw eggs alongside raw meat in 'high meat' diet threads.[13]

Protein. In the 1998 Evenepoel study, five ileostomy patients ate a 25 g portion of isotope-labelled egg protein cooked and, on another occasion, raw. True ileal digestibility averaged about 90.9 percent for cooked and about 51.3 percent for raw protein.[5] Reference works repeat these figures as roughly 51 and 91 percent bioavailability.[8] The authors concluded that heat treatment significantly improves digestibility.[5] Forum critics use this to argue that a raw egg delivers less usable protein than a cooked one; supporters reply that raw eggs are easier to consume in volume.[2]

Choline. Egg yolk is among the richest dietary sources of choline, with one hard-boiled large egg supplying about 147 mg against a US adequate intake of 550 mg per day for men and 425 mg for women.[14] Choline builds cell-membrane phospholipids and acetylcholine.[14] One looksmax.org poster argues that the only reason to eat raw eggs is choline, giving 150 mg raw against 120 mg cooked per egg and calling the difference small.[2]

Biotin and avidin. Avidin, found in egg white, binds biotin extremely tightly.[7] The effect called egg-white injury was traced in stages: W. G. Bateman reported toxic effects of high raw-white diets in 1916, Boas and Parsons showed in 1927 that rats fed white as their only protein lost hair and developed dermatitis and nerve dysfunction, and Paul Gyorgy showed in 1941 that avidin binding biotin was responsible.[7] Mild biotin deficiency is described as causing hair thinning, brittle nails and a facial rash.[7] Cooking above about 70 degrees Celsius largely removes avidin's binding ability.[6] Biotin itself is a cofactor in metabolic pathways including fatty acid synthesis and gluconeogenesis.[15]

Whole raw eggs also contain yolk biotin, and published animal and human cases of deficiency involve very large, sustained raw-white intakes, as described in the historical literature.[7] Proponents who drink a few raw eggs a day generally say this is not a worry; critics list it as a reason to cook.[2]

Salmonella can reach the egg interior from the hen during laying or contaminate the shell; heat at about 71 degrees Celsius kills it instantly, and in-shell pasteurisation uses roughly 57 degrees Celsius for about 75 minutes to reduce risk without cooking the egg.[8] A 2002 USDA estimate cited by Wikipedia put contamination at about one in 30,000 eggs.[8]

A 1988 JAMA paper described a more than sixfold rise in reported Salmonella Enteritidis infections in the northeastern United States between 1976 and 1986, with most outbreaks that had an identified food source linked to Grade A shell eggs or foods containing them.[16] A Dutch case-control study identified raw eggs as a predominant risk factor for Enteritidis infection.[17] The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates about 1.35 million Salmonella infections a year in the United States and says only about 1 in 30 is diagnosed.[18]

The FDA describes symptoms that usually begin 12 to 72 hours after infection and include diarrhoea, fever, abdominal cramps and vomiting, and says that in severe cases infection can spread to the bloodstream.[9] It advises that recipes using raw or undercooked eggs use shell eggs treated to destroy Salmonella or pasteurised egg products, and the same page lists children, older adults, pregnant women and immunocompromised people as at greater risk.[9]

Washing practices differ by region. US eggs are washed, which removes the natural cuticle, so refrigeration is recommended; European eggs are usually unwashed. In the UK, hens are vaccinated against Salmonella, and the Wikipedia article reports that eggs are considered safe for 21 days.[8] Pasteurised in-shell eggs, stamped with a mark such as a letter P in a circle, are sold in some countries, and the USDA says they can be eaten without cooking, though taste reviews of them are mixed.[19]

A published report described anaphylactic reactions to raw egg in people who had passed challenges with cooked egg, showing that heat can change how the immune system reacts to egg proteins.[20] Egg white allergy is among the most common food allergies in infants.[8]

Randomised trial. In the 2022 Maastricht trial, 45 resistance-trained young men completed one whole-body resistance session and then ate five raw eggs, five boiled eggs or a control breakfast. Muscle biopsies showed that myofibrillar protein synthesis rose by roughly 18 to 20 percent over control in both egg groups, with no significant difference between raw and boiled. Boiled eggs produced higher peak essential amino acid levels in blood than raw eggs.[10]
Digestibility study. The 1998 isotope study measured true ileal digestibility in ileostomy patients, finding about 51 percent for raw and about 91 percent for cooked egg protein.[5]

Safety and epidemiology. Research on raw egg intake is mostly food-safety work on Salmonella from eggs.[12][16][17] No studies found of raw egg consumption for long-term muscle gain, body composition or facial appearance outcomes.

Looksmax.org has numerous threads in which users describe drinking a dozen or more raw eggs at a time, ask how to tolerate the taste, discuss fermenting eggs, or cite claims about choline benefits.[3][13][21] One thread asks whether to switch from cooked to raw after months of eating six eggs a day, citing parasite concerns.[1] A thread titled 'Raw Eggs are a Meme' argues that raw eggs offer less protein and fewer bioavailable nutrients, and some replies say blending raw eggs into shakes is more convenient than cooking.[2]
Discussion sits within wider threads on bulking and high-protein diets, where eggs are a common whole-food staple and raw eggs are one option among many for hitting protein targets.

Related ideas include eating cooked whole eggs for protein and choline, using pasteurised liquid egg or egg-white products, raw milk and raw organ-meat 'ancestral' diets, and high-protein bulking diets.[11] Other practices overlap with biotin supplements, which are marketed for hair, skin and nails.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org raw eggs are posted as a protein-and-choline habit, sometimes in large numbers, and are also criticised as inefficient.[2][3][21]

claims.claim: Raw eggs are a convenient, nutrient-rich protein source.
Raw eggs build muscle just as well as cooked eggs.
